text: Llangadwaladr is a small village in south-west Anglesey, Wales, near the royal court of Aberffraw. Its church, dedicated to Cadwaladr, holds the Cadfan Stone, a seventh-century inscribed memorial in Latin to Cadfan ap Iago, king of Gwynedd, describing him as the wisest and most renowned of all kings. It is one of the earliest monuments of the kings of Gwynedd.

The Holy Crown of Hungary is the coronation crown of the Hungarian kings, traditionally linked with Stephen I, though its surviving form combines Byzantine enamel work of the later eleventh century with a Latin upper part. From the later Middle Ages it embodied the kingdom itself, and a king was not fully legitimate until crowned with it at Székesfehérvár. Since 2000 it has been displayed in the Hungarian Parliament building.

The Lex Manilia was a Roman law proposed by the tribune Gaius Manilius in 66 BCE that gave Pompey command of the war against Mithridates VI of Pontus and Tigranes of Armenia, with very wide powers in the east. Cicero spoke in its favour in his speech De imperio Cn. Pompei. Such extraordinary commands concentrated power in single generals and weakened the Republic.

Eratosthenes of Cyrene was a Greek scholar who became head of the Library of Alexandria under the Ptolemies. He made a remarkably close estimate of the Earth's circumference from the angle of the sun at Syene and Alexandria, drew a map of the known world with lines of latitude and longitude, and devised a method for finding prime numbers. His geography, quoted by Strabo, described Arabia and its peoples.

The College of Justice is the body of judges and lawyers of Scotland's supreme courts, founded by James V in 1532 with funds from the Scottish church approved by the pope. Its core is the Court of Session, the supreme civil court, whose judges are styled senators of the College of Justice. It gave Scotland a permanent professional central court and fostered a distinct Scots legal profession.

Lotan is a seven-headed sea serpent in the Ugaritic texts of the Late Bronze Age, called the fleeing serpent and the twisting serpent, and defeated by the storm god Baal and the goddess Anat. A servant of the sea god Yam, it embodies the forces of chaos that the storm god overcomes. The same epithets are applied to Leviathan in Isaiah 27:1, showing the debt of biblical poetry to Canaanite myth.

Ishpuini was king of Urartu in the late ninth century BCE, the son of Sarduri I. With his son Menua as co-ruler he introduced inscriptions in the Urartian language, organised the state cult of the god Haldi and extended Urartian influence to the sanctuary of Musasir, as recorded on the bilingual Kelishin stele. He laid the foundations for Urartu's expansion in the eighth century.

Dorchester-on-Thames is a village in Oxfordshire on the River Thame near its confluence with the Thames. A Roman small town, it lay at the heart of early West Saxon settlement, and in 635 Bishop Birinus baptised King Cynegils there and made it the seat of the first West Saxon bishopric. Later the seat of a Mercian bishopric until 1072, it keeps its large medieval abbey church.

Abdallah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh was an Arab commander and governor of Egypt from about 645 to 656 under the caliph Uthman, his foster-brother. In 652 he besieged Old Dongola, capital of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, but could not take it and concluded the Baqt, a treaty that governed Egyptian–Nubian relations for six centuries. He also led raids into north Africa and commanded at the naval victory over the Byzantines known as the Battle of the Masts.

The Rukun Negara ('Principles of the Nation') is Malaysia's national philosophy, proclaimed on 31 August 1970 after the racial riots of 13 May 1969 to foster unity among its peoples. Its five principles are belief in God, loyalty to king and country, the supremacy of the constitution, the rule of law, and courtesy and morality.

The 1936 Summer Olympics were held in Berlin in August 1936. The Nazi regime used them as a propaganda showcase, temporarily toning down open anti-Jewish measures, and introduced the torch relay from Olympia. The African-American athlete Jesse Owens won four gold medals, and Leni Riefenstahl's film Olympia recorded the Games.

Dolores Hidalgo is a town in the Mexican state of Guanajuato. On 16 September 1810 its parish priest, Miguel Hidalgo, rang the church bell and called his parishioners to revolt, the Cry of Dolores that began the Mexican War of Independence. The date is Mexico's national independence day, and the town, renamed in Hidalgo's honour, is regarded as the cradle of national independence.

Theophanes the Greek was a Byzantine painter of icons and frescoes who worked in the Russian lands from about the 1370s. His frescoes of 1378 in the Church of the Transfiguration on Ilyina Street in Novgorod are his only surviving securely attributed murals. In Moscow he worked with Andrei Rublev on the iconostasis of the Cathedral of the Annunciation in 1405, shaping the course of Russian icon painting.

Ares was the Greek god of war, a son of Zeus and Hera, identified by the Romans with Mars. Greek writers often placed his home in Thrace, and Herodotus reported that the Thracians worshipped gods he equated with Ares, Dionysus and Artemis. Unlike Athena, he embodied the violence and destruction of battle and was less honoured in cult than most of the Olympian gods.

Ballari, formerly Bellary, is a city in eastern Karnataka, India, known for the fort on the great granite rock that overlooks it. The surrounding region, rich in iron ore, has a long history: the earliest Pallava charters of the fourth century record grants of land there, and it later lay at the heart of the Vijayanagara Empire, whose capital Hampi is nearby.

Gunabhadra was a Digambara Jain monk and author of the ninth century, a disciple of Jinasena, working in the Rashtrakuta empire. He completed his teacher's unfinished Adipurana and wrote the Uttarapurana, which together form the Mahapurana, the Sanskrit history of the 63 illustrious persons of Jain tradition. He also wrote the Atmanushasana, a work on spiritual discipline.

Matagalpa is a city in the central highlands of Nicaragua and capital of the department of the same name, at the heart of the country's main coffee-growing region. Coffee spread there from the 1870s, encouraged by laws that transferred indigenous communal land to private owners and by grants to European settlers. These pressures provoked an indigenous revolt in 1881, which was suppressed by the government.

Derbyshire is a county in the East Midlands of England, including much of the Peak District. Its lead deposits were mined in Roman times, when lead pigs stamped with the name of the district were produced, and mining continued through the Middle Ages. In the Anglo-Saxon period it lay in the kingdom of Mercia, and in the 18th century the Derwent valley mills made it a cradle of the factory system.

The Thebaid was the southern region of ancient Egypt around Thebes, stretching from about Abydos to the First Cataract at Aswan. Under Roman rule it was an administrative district, the scene of a revolt against Roman taxation soon after the conquest, and from Diocletian's time a separate province. It is also known as a cradle of Christian monasticism.

The Cheka, the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission, was the first Soviet secret police, founded in December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky to fight counter-revolution and sabotage. During the Russian Civil War it carried out the Red Terror, with mass arrests, hostage-taking and executions without trial. In 1922 it was replaced by the GPU, a forerunner of the NKVD and the KGB.

Ameinocles was a Corinthian shipbuilder named by Thucydides, who records that he built four ships for the Samians about three hundred years before the end of the Peloponnesian War, that is around 704 BCE. Thucydides cites him in his account of Corinth's leading role in early Greek shipbuilding, and the passage is one of the earliest pieces of evidence for Greek naval technology.

Phra Phuttha Chinnarat is a gilded bronze seated Buddha image in Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat in Phitsanulok, Thailand, cast in the late Sukhothai style, probably in the fourteenth century. With its flame-shaped halo it is regarded as one of the most beautiful Buddha images in Thailand, and it served as a model for later images, including a copy at Wat Benchamabophit in Bangkok.

The Alaeddin Mosque is the main mosque of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in Konya, Turkey, standing on Alaeddin Hill at the heart of the city. Begun in the twelfth century and completed under Kayqubad I around 1220, it has a large hall of reused antique columns and a courtyard containing the tombs of several Seljuk sultans.

The Iranun are a people of the coast of Mindanao around Illana Bay in the southern Philippines, with communities also in Sabah. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Iranun fleets, allied with the Sulu Sultanate, were renowned as maritime raiders, attacking coasts from the Philippines to the Malay Peninsula and Indonesia and taking captives for the slave trade.

Guillaume-Henri Dufour was a Swiss general and engineer from Geneva. He commanded the federal army that defeated the Sonderbund in November 1847 with few casualties, paving the way for the federal state of 1848. He directed the first official topographic map of Switzerland, the Dufour map, and was a co-founder of the International Committee of the Red Cross. The highest Swiss peak, the Dufourspitze, is named after him.

The Mahavyutpatti is a Sanskrit–Tibetan dictionary compiled in imperial Tibet in the early ninth century, under royal patronage, to standardise the translation of Buddhist texts. Its thousands of entries fixed the Tibetan equivalents of Sanskrit terms, giving Tibetan translations of Indian scriptures their remarkable consistency. It is also a valuable source for Buddhist Sanskrit vocabulary.

The Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations was an international exhibition held in the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, London, from May to October 1851. Organised by Prince Albert and Henry Cole, it displayed manufactures and inventions from around the world, attracted about six million visitors and showcased Britain's industrial leadership.

The Montagne Sainte-Geneviève is a hill on the Left Bank of the Seine in the 5th arrondissement of Paris. It was the centre of Roman Lutetia, with its forum, and later took its name from the abbey of Saint Genevieve, the city's patron saint. Its schools made it the cradle of the University of Paris, and the Panthéon now stands on its summit.

Demeter was the Greek goddess of grain, agriculture and the fertility of the earth, and mother of Persephone. The myth of Persephone's abduction by Hades and Demeter's search for her explained the cycle of the seasons and lay at the heart of the Eleusinian Mysteries, the most famous mystery cult of Greece. Her sanctuaries were found throughout the Greek world, and the Romans identified her with Ceres.

Paestum is an ancient city in Campania in southern Italy, founded as the Greek colony of Poseidonia around 600 BCE. Taken by the Lucanians around 410 BCE and refounded as a Latin colony in 273 BCE, it is renowned for three well-preserved Doric temples and the painted Tomb of the Diver. It is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Albert III Achilles was a Hohenzollern prince, Margrave of Ansbach from 1440 and of Kulmbach from 1464, and Elector of Brandenburg from 1470. A renowned soldier and tournament fighter, he fought long wars against the city of Nuremberg and other neighbours. In 1473 he issued the Dispositio Achillea, which ruled that Brandenburg should pass undivided to the eldest son while the Franconian lands went to younger sons.

Telavi is a town in eastern Georgia, the main centre of Kakheti, on the slopes above the Alazani valley. It was a seat of the kings of Kakheti-Hereti in the 11th century and later of the Kingdom of Kakheti, and the palace of King Erekle II, built in the 18th century, survives within its walled royal compound. It lies at the heart of Georgia's chief wine region.

Brandenburg an der Havel is a city on the Havel in the German state of Brandenburg, west of Berlin. It began as Brenna, the chief stronghold of the Slavic Hevelli, where Otto I founded a bishopric in 948. Albert the Bear secured it in 1157, and it gave its name to the March of Brandenburg and, ultimately, to the modern state. Its cathedral island preserves medieval buildings.

Lorenzo de' Medici, called the Magnificent, was the effective ruler of the Republic of Florence from 1469 until his death. He survived the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478, in which his brother Giuliano was killed, and worked to keep peace among the Italian states through diplomacy. A poet and a patron of artists such as Botticelli and the young Michelangelo, he came to embody the Florentine Renaissance.

Lithuanian Jews, or Litvaks, were the Jewish community of the lands of the historic Grand Duchy of Lithuania, centred on Vilnius, known as the 'Jerusalem of Lithuania'. From the 18th century they were renowned for Talmudic scholarship, led by figures such as the Vilna Gaon, and for yeshivas such as Volozhin. About 90 to 95 per cent of the Jews of Lithuania were murdered in the Holocaust in 1941–1944.

Tyrifjorden is a large lake in Buskerud, eastern Norway, north-west of Oslo. Despite its name it is a freshwater lake, not a fjord. It lies at the heart of the Ringerike district, a petty kingdom of the Viking age, and drains southwards into the Drammen River.

Bar-Rakib was a king of Sam'al, an Aramaean kingdom in south-eastern Anatolia, in the later 8th century BCE. A loyal vassal of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III, he set up Aramaic inscriptions honouring his father Panamuwa II and boasting of his own palace building. His reliefs, including one showing him enthroned before a scribe, are among the best-known finds from the site at Zincirli.

Kilamuwa was a king of Sam'al, a kingdom in south-eastern Anatolia, in the later 9th century BCE. His inscription, carved in Phoenician on a stone slab found at Zincirli in 1902, boasts that he hired the king of Assyria against his enemies and improved the lot of his poorest subjects. It is one of the most important early royal inscriptions in a Northwest Semitic language.

Nyikang is the legendary founder and culture hero of the Shilluk people of South Sudan. According to tradition he led his people north along the White Nile and settled them on its west bank, becoming their first reth, or king. Each later reth was believed to embody his spirit, and he is venerated at shrines across Shilluk country.

Elena Ceaușescu (1916–1989) was the wife of the Romanian communist leader Nicolae Ceaușescu and from the 1970s the second most powerful person in the country, as a member of the party's top body and first deputy prime minister. Despite little formal schooling she was promoted as a world-renowned chemist. She was tried with her husband by a military tribunal and executed with him on 25 December 1989.

Sintra is a town in the hills west of Lisbon, Portugal. A castle built under Muslim rule crowns its ridge, and the town passed definitively to Portugal after Afonso I took Lisbon in 1147. Portuguese kings built the Sintra National Palace there, and 19th-century romantic buildings such as the Pena Palace helped make its cultural landscape a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995.

Pittheus was a legendary king of Troezen in Greek mythology, a son of Pelops and renowned for his wisdom. He arranged for his daughter Aethra to lie with the Athenian king Aegeus, and their son Theseus was born and raised at Troezen in his grandfather's house. Pausanias records that the people of Troezen showed his tomb and the seat from which he was said to have given judgement.

The Bill of Rights 1689 is an Act of the English Parliament that set out the terms on which William III and Mary II took the throne after the Glorious Revolution. It declared illegal the suspension of laws and taxation without Parliament's consent, forbade a standing army in peacetime without its approval, guaranteed free elections and freedom of speech in Parliament, and barred Catholics from the throne. It remains a cornerstone of the British constitution.

The Governor's Palace is a long palace building at the Maya city of Uxmal in Yucatán, Mexico, built on a huge artificial platform around 900–1000. About 100 metres long, its upper façade carries an intricate stone mosaic of fretwork, latticework and masks of the rain god, and it is often called the finest example of Puuc architecture. It is traditionally linked with the ruler Lord Chaak.

The Libro d'Oro, or Golden Book, was the official register of the patrician families of the Republic of Venice, recording the births and marriages that qualified men to sit in the Great Council. Kept from the early 16th century, it embodied the closed hereditary nobility created by the Serrata of 1297. Venetian territories such as Corfu kept their own golden books of local nobles. The Venetian book was publicly burned in 1797.

Montego Bay is a city on the north-west coast of Jamaica and the capital of the parish of St James. A centre of the sugar trade in the colonial period, it was at the heart of the 1831–1832 Christmas Rebellion of enslaved people led by Samuel Sharpe. In 1947 it hosted the conference on closer association of the British Caribbean colonies that led to the West Indies Federation. It is now Jamaica's main tourist centre.

Henan is a province of central China on the middle and lower Yellow River, with Zhengzhou as its capital. Often called the cradle of Chinese civilisation, it holds the Erlitou site, the Shang capitals at Zhengzhou and Anyang, and the old imperial capitals of Luoyang and Kaifeng. Many states of the Zhou period lay within it, and it remains one of China's most populous provinces.

Makimuku is an archaeological site in Sakurai, Nara Prefecture, Japan, at the foot of Mount Miwa. In the early 3rd century it grew into a large planned settlement with a major building complex and some of the earliest keyhole-shaped tombs, including Hashihaka. Many scholars see it as the centre of Queen Himiko's Yamatai or as the cradle of the Yamato kingship.

Haryana is a state of northern India surrounding Delhi on three sides, with Chandigarh, shared with Punjab, as its capital. The region includes Kurukshetra and Panipat, scenes of famous battles, and lay at the heart of ancient and medieval north Indian states. It was carved out of the Indian state of Punjab in 1966 as a mainly Hindi-speaking state and is among the most prosperous in India.

Zhang Zhidong was a Chinese official of the late Qing dynasty who advocated controlled reform and the modernisation of the army, serving as viceroy of Huguang from 1889. He ordered an iron and steel plant from England, which began production in 1894 but made substantial losses, and founded a mint, mills and factories. His Exhortation to Study of 1898 summed up his relatively conservative reform in the phrase "Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application". He took a leading role in abolishing the imperial examination in 1905.

Crucible steel is steel made by melting iron, often with fluxes, in a crucible, which allows precise control of its carbon content; it was first developed in southern India and Sri Lanka by the wootz process, with material as early as 300 BCE. Wootz steel was traded widely and became famous in the Middle East as Damascus steel. In England, Benjamin Huntsman of Sheffield developed it in parallel from 1740, making the first fully homogeneous steel; within a century Sheffield's output rose from about 200 to over 80,000 tonnes a year.

A bicycle is a pedal-driven, single-track vehicle with two wheels attached to a frame, one behind the other. Its first form, Karl von Drais’s two-wheeled running machine without pedals, was shown in Mannheim in 1817, and pedals on an enlarged front wheel were added in France in the early 1860s. The upright safety bicycle has changed little since the first chain-driven model of around 1885, and it gave women unprecedented mobility. Ball bearings, pneumatic tyres, chain-driven sprockets and tension-spoked wheels were first invented for the bicycle.

The trireme was an ancient Mediterranean galley driven by three banks of oars with one man to each oar, first referred to at the end of the 8th century BCE; scholars are divided on whether it came from Greece or Phoenicia. Fast and agile, with a crew of about 200 including 170 rowers, it was the dominant warship of the Mediterranean from the 7th to the 4th centuries BCE. Triremes played a vital role in the Persian Wars, and a fleet of over 200 was the foundation of Athenian power.

Alchemy is a philosophical and protoscientific tradition whose common aims were turning base metals into gold and making an elixir of immortality; in its Western form it is first attested in texts written in Greco-Roman Egypt in the first centuries CE, with Alexandria as its centre. Chinese and Indian alchemy appear to have been mostly independent in their earlier stages. Alchemy reached Latin Europe through translations from Arabic from 1144 onwards, and the Latin tradition played a significant role in the development of early modern chemistry and medicine.

Quinine is an alkaloid from the bark of the cinchona tree, native to Peru, used to treat malaria; extracts of the bark were used against malaria from at least 1632, and the substance itself was first isolated in 1820 by the French researchers Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou. Cinchona bark, known as Jesuit's bark or Peruvian bark, became one of the most valuable goods shipped from Peru to Europe. Quinine remained the antimalarial drug of choice until the 1940s and played a significant role in the European colonisation of Africa.

The city-state, a city that governs itself and its countryside, was among the earliest forms of state and one of the most inventive. From Uruk and Athens to Kilwa, Venice and Lübeck it fostered citizenship, commerce and republican thought, though its small size left it prone to faction and conquest; Singapore, Monaco and Vatican City carry it on today.

Amartya Sen is an Indian economist and philosopher, born in 1933 in Santiniketan, Bengal, British India, and named by Rabindranath Tagore. He received the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in 1998 for his contributions to welfare economics, and has also worked on social choice theory, development economics and the measures of well-being of countries. In Poverty and Famines (1981) he argued that famine comes not only from a lack of food but from inequalities in the mechanisms for distributing it. He has taught in England and the United States since 1972, was master of Trinity College, Cambridge, and received the Bharat Ratna in 1999.

text: William Morris was an English textile designer, poet, artist, writer and socialist activist associated with the British Arts and Crafts movement and the revival of traditional British textile arts. In 1861 he founded the decorative arts firm Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. with Edward Burne-Jones, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Philip Webb and others, designing tapestries, wallpaper, fabrics, furniture and stained glass; from 1875 it was Morris & Co. His poems and novels, among them the utopian News from Nowhere (1890), helped to establish the modern fantasy genre. He founded the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings in 1877, the Socialist League in 1884 and the Kelmscott Press in 1891.

Lin Biao was a Chinese military commander and politician, ranked third among the Ten Marshals of the People's Republic of China. Pivotal to the Communist victory in the Chinese Civil War, he commanded the Liaoshen and Pingjin campaigns and led the People's Liberation Army into Beijing. Minister of National Defense from 1959, he directed the compilation of the Quotations from Chairman Mao Zedong, the Little Red Book, and helped build Mao Zedong's cult of personality; in 1966 he was designated Mao's sole successor. He died in 1971 when his aircraft crashed near Öndörkhaan, Mongolia, in circumstances that remain disputed, and was posthumously condemned as a traitor.

Emma Goldman was a Russian-born anarchist revolutionary, political activist and writer who played a pivotal role in the development of anarchist political philosophy in North America and Europe. Born in Kaunas to a Lithuanian Jewish family, she immigrated to the United States in 1885 and lectured on anarchism, women's rights and social issues; with Alexander Berkman she planned the 1892 attempt on the life of Henry Clay Frick. She founded the journal Mother Earth in 1906, was jailed in 1917 for conspiring against the draft and was deported to Russia in December 1919. After the Kronstadt rebellion she denounced the Soviet Union, and later supported the anarchist revolution in Spain.

Sir Isaiah Berlin was a British social and political theorist, philosopher and historian of ideas, born into a Russian-Jewish family in Riga in 1909. As a boy in Petrograd he witnessed the Russian Revolution, and in 1921 his family moved to England. From 1957 to 1967 he was Chichele Professor of Social and Political Theory at Oxford; his inaugural lecture, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958), set negative liberty, the absence of interference, against positive liberty, self-mastery. He became the founding president of Wolfson College, Oxford, in 1966, and his work on liberal theory and value pluralism, and his opposition to Marxism and communism, has had a lasting influence.

Édouard Manet was a French painter, one of the first 19th-century artists to paint modern life and a pivotal figure in the transition from Realism to Impressionism. Born in Paris in 1832, he studied under the academic painter Thomas Couture from 1850 to 1856 and copied Velázquez and Titian in the Louvre. His Luncheon on the Grass (1863) and Olympia (1865) caused great controversy with critics and the Academy but were praised by progressive artists, and they are considered to mark the start of modern art. His last major work, A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, hung in the Salon in 1882; he died in Paris in April 1883, 11 days after his left foot was amputated because of gangrene.

Mustafa Reşid Pasha was an Ottoman statesman and diplomat, born in Constantinople, known best as the chief architect of the Tanzimat reforms. He served as ambassador to France and the United Kingdom, became minister for foreign affairs in 1837 and played a leading role in the authorship of the Edict of Gülhane of 1839, which opened the Tanzimat era. Between 1845 and 1857 he held the office of Grand Vizier six times, setting up commercial courts and codes on French models, a committee of education meant to reduce the influence of the ulema, and an Academy of Sciences in 1852. He died of a heart attack in 1858, and his protégés Fuad Pasha and Mehmed Emin Âli Pasha carried the reforms on.

Al-Nasir Hasan was a Mamluk sultan of Egypt, a son of al-Nasir Muhammad, who reigned twice, in 1347–1351 and 1354–1361. Installed at the age of 12, he was at first a ceremonial ruler under the senior emirs and was deposed in 1351 when he tried to assert his authority. Restored by a coup of the emirs Shaykhu and Sirghitmish, he purged the leading emirs through imprisonment, exile and execution and gave high ranks to the awlad al-nas, the descendants of mamluks, on a scale unprecedented in the sultanate. He was killed in 1361 by one of his own mamluks, Yalbugha al-Umari; the Sultan Hasan Mosque-Madrasa in Cairo, begun in 1357, was completed in 1363.

Takedda was a town and former kingdom in present-day Niger, west of the Aïr Massif; the archaeological site of Azelik wan Birni is believed to hold its ruins. Founded by the Sanhaja, a Berber tribal confederation of the Maghreb, the Tuareg-controlled kingdom played a prominent role in long-distance trade in the 14th century, chiefly because of its copper mines. Ibn Battuta visited it in 1353 on his return from the Mali Empire, and Mansa Sakoura of Mali took his army east to subjugate the copper-producing area. Excavations by the French archaeologist Danilo Grébénart have found evidence of copperworking at the site dating to the first millennium BCE.

Praskovia Kovalyova-Zhemchugova was a Russian serf actress and soprano opera singer, born into the family of a serf blacksmith owned by the Sheremetevs, probably in the province of Yaroslavl. Trained for the opera company of Count Pyotr Sheremetev and his son Nikolai, she debuted at the serf theatre of Kuskovo in 1779 and from 1780 appeared under the stage name Zhemchugova, "the Pearl". Her most important role was Eliane in Grétry's Les Mariages samnites, which she sang for 12 years and performed for Empress Catherine II in 1787. Nikolai Sheremetev freed her from serfdom in 1798 and married her in secret in 1801; she died in 1803, weeks after giving birth to their son Dmitry.

Louis Armstrong was an American jazz trumpeter, cornetist and singer from New Orleans, among the most influential figures in jazz, who shifted the music's focus from collective improvisation to solo performance. Raised in poverty, he followed his mentor King Oliver to Chicago in 1922, and his Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings from 1925 showcased his solos. He was one of the first African-American entertainers to reach wide white and international audiences, toured Africa, Europe and Asia for the US State Department, and spoke out publicly during the Little Rock school desegregation crisis of 1957. His recording of Hello, Dolly! reached No. 1 in 1964. He died in Queens, New York, in 1971.

A loom is a device for weaving cloth and tapestry that holds the warp threads under tension while the weft threads are passed over and under them. The earliest evidence of a horizontal loom is a picture on a pottery dish from ancient Egypt dated to 4400 BCE, showing a frame loom with treadles that left the weaver's hands free to pass and beat the weft. The warp-weighted loom, whose warp is kept taut by hanging weights, may go back to the Neolithic. The drawloom for patterned silk is first confirmed by fabrics from the State of Chu of about 400 BCE; it sped up Chinese silk weaving and was introduced to Persia, India and Europe.

Organ transplantation is the removal of an organ or tissue from one body and its placement in another, to replace a damaged or missing function. The first transplant in the modern sense was performed in 1883 by the Swiss surgeon Theodor Kocher, who reversed the symptoms that followed the complete removal of the thyroid by implanting thyroid tissue. Alexis Carrel's techniques for joining blood vessels, from the early 1900s, laid the groundwork for later transplant surgery, but rejection defeated most attempts until Joseph Murray's kidney transplant between identical twins in Boston in 1954. Christiaan Barnard performed the first human-to-human heart transplant in 1967.

The Akathist Hymn takes its name from the Greek for "unseated": while it is chanted, the congregation stands in reverence, and only the aged and the infirm sit. In Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic services, where sitting, standing and bowing follow intricate rules, standing is required of all only for the Gospel, the Six Psalms of Matins and the akathists.

"Abide with Me" is a Christian hymn by the Anglican cleric Henry Francis Lyte (1793–1847). Lyte was a curate in County Wexford from 1815 to 1818, where he often preached at the church in Killurin and came under the lasting influence of its rector, the Reverend Abraham Swanne; he was later vicar of All Saints' Church in Brixham, Devon.

Dekulakization was a campaign of repression in the Soviet Union against the so-called kulaks, a loosely defined category of supposedly wealthy or exploitative peasants, begun after Stalin announced the liquidation of the kulaks as a class on 27 December 1929. It aimed to break resistance to collectivization and to supply forced labour for Siberia, the Urals, Kazakhstan and the North. Between 2.1 and 2.3 million people were deported to special settlements in 1930–1933 and 20,000 to 30,000 executed by troiki; Manfred Hildermeier estimates 530,000 to 600,000 deaths, excluding the famine. The deportations became a cornerstone of the Gulag and helped bring about the famine of 1930–1933.

Emperor Daigo was the 60th emperor of Japan according to the traditional order of succession, reigning from 897 to 930. The eldest son of Emperor Uda, he was born a subject named Minamoto no Korezane, because his grandfather Emperor Kōkō had demoted his sons from the imperial ranks, and became an imperial prince only in 887. The highlight of his 34-year reign was that he ruled by himself without a Fujiwara regent, though he was part Fujiwara himself; in his reign Ki no Tsurayuki presented the Kokin Wakashū. Falling ill in 930, he abdicated, became a monk and died, and was buried at Daigo-ji, which gave him his posthumous name.

Gopal Krishna Gokhale was an Indian political leader and social reformer of the independence movement, a senior leader of the Indian National Congress and the political guru of Mahatma Gandhi. Born into a Chitpavan Brahmin family, he graduated from Elphinstone College in 1884 and joined the Congress in 1889 as a protégé of Mahadev Govind Ranade. He led its moderate faction, which sought reform through existing institutions, against Bal Gangadhar Tilak's agitation, a rivalry that split the party at Surat in 1907. As Congress president in 1905 he founded the Servants of India Society to expand Indian education, and he played a leading role in the Morley-Minto Reforms.

The Helvetii were a Celtic tribe or tribal confederation that occupied most of the Swiss Plateau when they came into contact with the Roman Republic in the 1st century BCE. They had no kings but seem to have been ruled by a class of noblemen. In 58 BCE they burned their homes and set out to settle in southwestern Gaul, a migration that served as a catalyst for Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul; defeated near Bibracte, they were sent back to rebuild their homes, and Caesar's own figures, which modern scholars think too high, claim only about 30 percent survived. Subjugated after 52 BCE and largely Romanised by the 2nd century, they were later assimilated by the Alemanni and Burgundians.

A shōen was a private estate or manor in Japan from about the 8th to the 15th century, often tax-free and autonomous, whose rise undermined the power of the emperor. The estates grew from lands assigned to shrines and temples or granted by the emperor, and from fields reclaimed under laws of 723 and 743 that let reclaimers keep them, eroding the ritsuryō system. Peasants commended their land to temples, shrines and court nobles to escape taxes, and by the end of the Heian period virtually all land in Japan was shōen. The estates fostered a local military class; stewards appointed under the Kamakura shogunate weakened their lords, and the system ended as villages came under daimyō.

The White Sea–Baltic Canal is a ship canal in Russia, opened on 2 August 1933, that runs 227 kilometres from the White Sea to Lake Onega and so to the Baltic Sea. It was the first major Soviet project built with forced labour: Gulag inmates dug it in twenty months between 1931 and 1933, almost entirely by hand, and between 12,000 and 25,000 of them died according to official records. Presented as a showcase of the first five-year plan and of convicts 'reforging' themselves through labour, it was praised in a book compiled by a brigade of 120 writers and artists organised by Maxim Gorky. Yet at 3.5 metres deep it was too shallow for most seagoing ships.

Santa Claus is a legendary figure originating in Western Christian culture who is said to bring gifts on the night of Christmas Eve. The figure derives from folklore surrounding Saint Nicholas, the 4th-century Greek bishop of Myra and patron saint of children, and from the Dutch Sinterklaas, whose legend settlers brought to 17th-century New Amsterdam; it also merged with the English Father Christmas. The name was first used in the United States press in 1773. The 1823 poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas", with its sleigh pulled by flying reindeer, laid the foundation for the modern image, which the cartoonist Thomas Nast helped to define in Harper's Weekly from 1863.

The Great Frost, as it was known in England, or Le Grand Hiver in France, was an extraordinarily cold winter in Europe in 1708–1709, the coldest European winter of the past 500 years. William Derham recorded a low of −12 °C at Upminster, near London, on the night of 5 January 1709. France was particularly hard hit: the famine that followed is estimated to have caused 600,000 deaths by the end of 1710. During the Great Northern War, winter storms and frosts killed thousands in the Swedish army invading Russia, contributing to the Russian victory at Poltava the following summer.

Apollo 8 was the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and the first human spaceflight to reach the Moon, flown from 21 to 27 December 1968. Its three astronauts, Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders, travelled 68 hours to the Moon and orbited it ten times without landing; they were the first humans to see and photograph its far side and an Earthrise. On Christmas Eve they read the first ten verses of the Book of Genesis in a television broadcast. The mission, the first crewed launch of the Saturn V rocket, ended with a splashdown in the northern Pacific Ocean and paved the way for Apollo 11 in July 1969.

Teotihuacan grew out of farming villages in the Teotihuacan Valley, a side valley in the north-east of the Basin of Mexico, well watered by springs and close to major sources of obsidian. In the last centuries BCE it was one of several growing centres in the basin, with Cuicuilco in the south as its main rival. Volcanic activity helped to shift this balance: eruptions of Popocatépetl, probably in the first century CE, displaced communities to the east, and the eruption of Xitle buried Cuicuilco under lava, although the date of that eruption is debated and may be considerably later. Teotihuacan drew in much of the basin’s population, and during the Tzacualli phase (c. 1–150 CE) it grew with remarkable speed. The Pyramid of the Sun, some 65 metres high, and early stages of the Pyramid of the Moon were raised in this period, and the city was laid out along the Avenue of the Dead on a grid oriented about 15.5 degrees east of north. Around 200–250 CE the Feathered Serpent Pyramid was built inside the vast enclosure known as the Ciudadela. By about 250 CE the city covered some 20 square kilometres and housed perhaps 100,000 people, making it one of the largest cities in the world. Its original name is unknown; Teotihuacan is the Nahuatl name later given to it by the Aztecs.

The empire, known to its people as Tawantinsuyu, the four parts together, may have held around ten million people, although estimates vary widely. Society rested on the ayllu, a kin-based community that held land collectively and shared labour, and on the Andean ideal of reciprocity. The state claimed rights over land, dividing it among the Inca state, the religion and the communities. Instead of taxes in goods or money, households owed labour, the mita: they worked state and temple fields, served in armies, built roads and buildings, and spun and wove. Its produce filled thousands of storehouses, or qollqa, which fed soldiers, officials and workers and supplied the state’s generosity at feasts. Specialists stood outside the normal system: the yanakuna, retainers bound to the nobility and the state, and the aqllakuna, chosen women who wove fine cloth and brewed maize beer, or chicha. Cloth was among the most valued goods. Agriculture combined maize grown on irrigated terraces with potatoes, quinoa and other crops of the high plateau, alongside herds of llamas and alpacas. Long-distance markets played a small role compared with redistribution by the state. Religion centred on the sun god Inti, honoured at the Coricancha in Cusco, alongside the creator Viracocha, local sacred places called huacas, and the mummies of past rulers.

New Spain was the most valuable part of the Spanish Empire and a hinge of the first global economy. Its silver, coined in the Mexico City mint as the real de a ocho or Spanish dollar, circulated from Europe to China and became a standard trade coin across the world, later serving as a model for the currencies of the United States and China. The Manila galleons, sailing between Acapulco and Manila from 1565 to 1815, connected the Americas and Asia directly for two and a half centuries. Crops, animals and techniques were exchanged across the Atlantic and Pacific, carrying maize, cacao and chillies outward and introducing wheat, cattle, horses and sugar cane into Mexico. Culturally, New Spain produced a distinctive baroque civilisation: the cathedrals of Mexico City and Puebla, the poet and scholar Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, the polymath Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora, and the Royal University of Mexico, founded in 1551. Indigenous and Spanish traditions mixed in religion, art and language, while the Virgin of Guadalupe became a lasting symbol. The viceroyalty shaped the borders, legal systems and cities of modern Mexico and Central America, and left Spanish place names, missions and law across the south-western United States, from Texas to California, as well as a lasting Hispanic and Catholic imprint on the Philippines.

New France shaped the map and peoples of North America far beyond its small population. French explorers charted much of the interior: Louis Jolliet and Jacques Marquette descended the Mississippi in 1673, René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle reached its mouth in 1682 and claimed Louisiana for Louis XIV, and the La Vérendrye family pushed west towards the prairies in the 1730s and 1740s. Posts and missions such as Detroit, founded in 1701, Mobile and New Orleans, founded in 1718, became lasting cities. French alliances with Native nations created a distinctive world of trade, intermarriage and diplomacy around the Great Lakes, which the historian Richard White called the middle ground. The Great Peace of Montreal of 1701, signed by about forty Native nations, ended a century of war with the Iroquois. The colony’s most enduring legacy is French Canada. Its language, Catholic faith, civil law and seigneurial landholding survived the British conquest and were guaranteed by the Quebec Act of 1774. Today some seven million French-speaking Quebecers and francophone communities across Canada trace their origins largely to the roughly 10,000 French immigrants who settled in the St Lawrence valley. The Métis of western Canada and the French heritage of Louisiana, together with the Cajuns descended from Acadians exiled after 1755, are further legacies.

New France was France’s North American empire, which from Quebec and Montreal reached through the Great Lakes to Louisiana by means of fur-trade alliances with Native nations; thinly settled and conquered by Britain in the Seven Years War, it left French Canada as its lasting legacy.

Gran Colombia was the military engine of independence in northern and western South America. Its armies and generals freed not only Venezuela, New Granada and Quito but also Peru and Upper Peru, which became Bolivia, and the union gave Bolívar the base for his wider plans. In 1826 he convened the Congress of Panama, the first attempt at a league of Spanish American republics; only Gran Colombia ratified its treaties, but it is often cited as a forerunner of later inter-American cooperation. The United States recognised the republic in 1822, among the first Latin American states it recognised, and Britain concluded a commercial treaty with it in 1825. The republic’s laws on manumission, education and the Church set patterns followed by its successor states, and its divisions between centralists and federalists, and between civilians and military caudillos, shaped their politics for the rest of the century. The memory of the union survives in symbols: the national flags of Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador all descend from the yellow, blue and red tricolour of Francisco de Miranda adopted by the republic. Bolívar’s dream of unity has been invoked repeatedly since, most prominently by Hugo Chávez, who renamed Venezuela the Bolivarian Republic in 1999.

text: The federation was the only time the five Central American states have been united as a sovereign country, and its failure shaped the region’s history. Its collapse left five small republics, each vulnerable to foreign intervention, from the American filibuster William Walker in Nicaragua in the 1850s to the repeated interventions of the United States in the twentieth century. Yet the ideal of union proved remarkably persistent. Further attempts followed throughout the nineteenth century, including a short-lived confederation in the 1840s, the Guatemalan president Justo Rufino Barrios’s attempt to impose union by force, which ended with his death at the Battle of Chalchuapa in 1885, and the Greater Republic of Central America of 1896–1898. In the twentieth century unionism lived on in the Central American Court of Justice of 1907, the Organisation of Central American States of 1951, the Central American Common Market of 1960 and the Central American Integration System founded in 1991. The federation’s symbols endure: the blue and white bands of its flag survive in the flags of all five former states, and the five volcanoes of its coat of arms appear on the arms of El Salvador and Nicaragua. Morazán is honoured as a national hero across the region, especially in Honduras and El Salvador.

The Republic of Panama’s significance is inseparable from the Panama Canal, opened on 15 August 1914, which shortened the sea voyage between New York and San Francisco by some 13,000 kilometres and transformed world shipping, naval strategy and the trade of the Pacific coast of the Americas. The canal was also the most conspicuous symbol of United States power in Latin America. Panama’s independence, won under the protection of American warships, became a classic example of ‘big stick’ diplomacy, and Theodore Roosevelt later boasted that he had taken the isthmus. Colombia accepted the loss only after the Thomson–Urrutia Treaty, ratified by the United States in 1921, paid it an indemnity of 25 million dollars. The campaign for sovereignty over the Canal Zone, culminating in the riots of January 1964 and the Torrijos–Carter Treaties, won wide support in Latin America and the Non-Aligned Movement, and the peaceful transfer of the canal in 1999 is often cited as a successful negotiated end to a colonial enclave. The construction of the canal also advanced tropical medicine, as Gorgas’s campaign demonstrated mosquito control on a large scale. Panama’s open ship registry, dollarised economy and offshore banking have given it an outsized place in global trade and finance, and figures such as the singer and politician Rubén Blades and the boxer Roberto Durán are known far beyond the isthmus.

The Western Zhou kings maintained two large standing forces mentioned in bronze inscriptions: the Six Armies of the West, stationed in the Wei River valley, and the Eight Armies of Chengzhou in the east, which may have included former Shang troops. Armies combined chariots with infantry armed with dagger-axes, spears and bows. Expansion was strongest in the first century of the dynasty. King Wu and the Duke of Zhou conquered the Shang heartland, and King Kang and King Zhao campaigned east into Shandong and south towards the Huai and Han rivers; the Xiao Yu ding inscription records a victory over the Guifang with thousands of captives. King Zhao's southern expedition against Chu, around 957 BCE, ended in disaster: the king died near the Han River, and later texts say the Six Armies were lost. Thereafter the Zhou were mostly on the defensive. The Huaiyi of the south-east and the Xianyun of the north-west became persistent enemies in the ninth century BCE. King Xuan (r. 827–782 BCE) restored Zhou military prestige with campaigns against the Xianyun, recorded on vessels such as the Duoyou ding and the Guoji Zi Bai pan, and against the Huaiyi. The regional lords played a growing role in defence, and their armies, especially those of the State of Jin, the State of Qin and the State of Zheng, eventually outweighed the king's.
The vast southern kingdom of the middle Yangtze, whose distinctive culture produced the Songs of Chu and which was Qin's most formidable rival.

The State of Qin rose from a horse-breeding frontier fief to the most formidable power of the Warring States, and the bureaucratic, legal and military institutions it forged under Shang Yang became, through its unification of China in 221 BCE, the foundations of two thousand years of imperial government.

Like the Xiongnu, the Yuezhi fought as mounted archers, and the Shiji credits them with between 100,000 and 200,000 archers, a figure that conveys their reputation rather than an exact count. Their wars were dominated by the rise of the Xiongnu. Modu escaped from captivity among them, seized power among the Xiongnu in 209 BCE and turned on the Yuezhi; around 176 BCE a Xiongnu letter to the Han court boasted that they had been crushed. The chanyu Laoshang later killed the Yuezhi king and made his skull into a drinking cup. The main body, afterwards called the Greater Yuezhi, then moved west to the Ili valley and Zhetysu, where they defeated the Saka and drove their king south. There they were attacked by the Wusun under their ruler, the kunmo, whose father had been killed, according to the Han shu, by the Yuezhi. Defeated again, they marched south-west through Fergana and, probably in the 130s BCE, crossed into Bactria, overwhelming what remained of Greek rule north of the Hindu Kush. When Zhang Qian reached them, sent by Emperor Wu of Han to propose an alliance against the Xiongnu, they had no wish for revenge and declined. Their later wars are almost invisible until the Kushan conquests.

Baekje's core lay in the fertile plains of the Han, Geum and Yeongsan river basins, where rice grown in irrigated paddies, together with millet and barley, formed the basis of the economy. Society was led by a small group of great families; the Chinese Sui shu names eight leading clans, including the Sa, Yeon, Hae, Jin and Mok, who supplied the highest officials and royal consorts. Below them stood free farmers liable to taxes, military service and corvée labour, and unfree people. Buddhism, brought from the Eastern Jin by the monk Marananta in 384, became the faith of the court, and the Sabi period saw great temples such as Jeongnimsa, whose five-storey stone pagoda still stands, and Mireuksa at Iksan, one of the largest temple complexes of its age, whose reliquary inscription dates its western pagoda to 639. Baekje craftsmen were renowned: the tomb of King Muryeong at Gongju, found intact in 1971, yielded gold crown ornaments, jewellery and Chinese ceramics, and the gilt-bronze incense burner discovered at Neungsan-ri in 1993 is among the masterpieces of East Asian metalwork. Sea routes linked Baekje with the southern Chinese courts, the Gaya states and the Japanese archipelago, bringing silks, ceramics and books from China and carrying Baekje goods, scholars and artisans to Japan.

Baekje's most enduring influence lay across the sea in Japan. Its close alliance with the Yamato court, sealed by exchanges of princes and envoys, made it a main route by which Chinese-derived learning, Buddhism and technology reached the Japanese archipelago. Japanese chronicles relate that the scholar Wani came from Baekje bringing the Analects and, anachronistically, the Thousand Character Classic, and that King Seong sent a Buddhist image and sutras to the Yamato court, in 552 according to the Nihon shoki, though another Japanese source gives 538, the date most often preferred today. Baekje monks, carpenters, tile-makers, painters and physicians helped build Japan's first great temples, including Asuka-dera. The Seven-Branched Sword kept at the Isonokami Shrine, inscribed with a date usually read as 369, is generally interpreted as a gift from a Baekje king to a Wa ruler. In Korea, Baekje's art, marked by gentle Buddhist sculpture such as the rock-carved triad at Seosan, and its stone pagodas influenced Silla and later Korean styles. After 660 thousands of Baekje refugees, including members of the royal family, settled in Japan, where the prince Zenkō received the surname Kudara no Konikishi and refugee experts helped build Korean-style mountain fortresses. The Baekje Historic Areas at Gongju, Buyeo and Iksan joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2015.

The Kushan period was decisive for the history of Buddhism and of Asian art. Under Kushan rule the workshops of Gandhara, drawing on Hellenistic models, and those of Mathura, rooted in Indian traditions, produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form, a development that shaped Buddhist sculpture from Afghanistan to Japan. Buddhist tradition remembers Kanishka as a great patron: his stupa at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri near Peshawar was among the wonders of the Buddhist world, admired by Chinese pilgrims, and its bronze relic casket, inscribed with Kanishka's name, was excavated in 1908–1909. Tradition also links Kanishka with a Buddhist council in Kashmir and with the poet Ashvaghosha, though both associations are uncertain. Monks from the Kushan lands carried Buddhist texts and Mahayana ideas along the Silk Road; Lokaksema, a Kushan monk active in Luoyang in the 170s and 180s, made some of the earliest Chinese translations of Mahayana sutras. Kushan gold coinage served as a model for the Kushano-Sasanians, the Kidarites and the Gupta Empire, whose early gold coins adapt Kushan designs, and Kushan titles and prestige were claimed by later rulers of the region. Bactrian, raised to an imperial language by Kanishka, remained in written use in the region until about the 9th century.
Kushan coins show a remarkable mix of gods, from the Iranian Mithra and the goddess Nana to Shiva, Heracles and the Buddha, labelled in Bactrian as Boddo.

The Eastern Jin carried the Jin dynasty south of the Yangtze after the fall of northern China, preserved its institutions and aristocratic culture at Jiankang, repelled the Former Qin at the Fei River in 383, and fostered the calligraphy, poetry and southern Buddhism that shaped Chinese civilisation for centuries.

The Rouran Khaganate's most lasting legacy is the steppe political tradition it handed on. The titles khagan, for the supreme ruler, and khatun, for his consort, became established at the Rouran court and were taken over by the Turkic Khaganate, which arose among the Rouran's own subjects, and later by the Uyghurs, the Khazars and the Mongols. The Turks also inherited the Rouran pattern of a royal clan ruling a confederation of tribes from the Mongolian steppe and extracting tribute from China and the oasis cities. The Rouran also shaped the history of northern China: the long struggle against them encouraged the Northern Wei to keep a heavily militarised frontier, and the Six Garrisons built to contain them became the centre of the great revolt of the 520s that broke the Northern Wei apart. In the west Rouran influence reached Turfan, the Tarim oases and possibly the Hephthalites. The fate of the Rouran after 555 has prompted a long debate. Byzantine writers record that the Avars who arrived on the Black Sea steppe around 557 were fleeing the Turks, and some historians identify them, or their ruling group, with Rouran refugees; others reject the link. Recent ancient DNA studies of early Avar elite burials in Hungary found ancestry closely matching populations of the Mongolian steppe, which some researchers see as supporting a Rouran connection.

Goryeo left a lasting mark on Korean identity. By uniting the Later Three Kingdoms and absorbing refugees from Balhae, it fixed the idea of a single kingdom covering most of the peninsula, and its name, carried abroad by merchants, became the Western name Korea. Kim Bu-sik's Samguk sagi of 1145, the oldest surviving Korean history, and the monk Iryeon's Samguk yusa of the 1280s have shaped how Koreans see their ancient past ever since. The Tripitaka Koreana, the Buddhist canon carved on more than 81,000 woodblocks between 1236 and 1251 to win divine protection against the Mongols, replaced an earlier set burned by them in 1232; it is preserved at Haeinsa temple and recognised by UNESCO. Goryeo printers also used movable metal type: the Jikji, a collection of Seon Buddhist teachings printed at Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, and literary sources record metal-type printing in Goryeo earlier in the thirteenth century. Inlaid celadon is regarded as one of the summits of East Asian ceramics and was much imitated in later Korean wares. Neo-Confucianism, which entered Goryeo under Yuan rule through scholars such as An Hyang, produced the reform-minded officials who later founded Joseon, and Joseon kept much of Goryeo's administrative framework and its capital region.

The Ghaznavids had a deep influence on the cultures of Iran, Afghanistan and South Asia. Their court helped make New Persian a language of imperial power far beyond its Iranian homeland. Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh, the national epic of Iran, around 1010 and presented it to Mahmud, although the story that the sultan rewarded him poorly is a later legend that cannot be verified. The scholar al-Biruni, brought to Ghazni after the conquest of Khwarazm, travelled in the Indian borderlands and wrote his Kitab ta'rikh al-Hind, a study of Indian religion, philosophy and science that is among the most remarkable works of medieval scholarship, and dedicated his astronomical treatise al-Qanun al-Mas'udi to Mas'ud. Bayhaqi's history is a classic of Persian prose, and the poet Sana'i dedicated his Hadiqat al-haqiqa to Bahram Shah. By annexing the Punjab and making Lahore a centre of Persian culture, where the Sufi Ali Hujwiri wrote the Kashf al-mahjub, the Ghaznavids prepared the ground for the Ghurids, the Delhi Sultanate and centuries of Persianate Muslim rule in India. Their raids, above all the sack of Somnath, became central to later memory: Muslim chroniclers celebrated Mahmud as a holy warrior, while in modern India the raids became a symbol of iconoclasm, a contested memory examined by the historian Romila Thapar.
